Text | jemand

Editing | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

Editor’s note: Metamaterials really have been one of the hottest research fields of the first two decades of the 21st century. After all, who could say no to Harry Potter’s Invisibility Cloak, and what country wouldn’t want a true “black hole in the ocean” submarine (the nickname of Russia’s famously quiet Kilo-class boats)? In this article, the author introduces research groups working on acoustic metamaterials and shares some thoughts on metamaterial research.

The research groups

This section introduces some of the groups working on acoustic metamaterials and topological structures, and their work. Space and my own limited experience mean it cannot be comprehensive or detailed, so I ask readers’ indulgence, and comments and suggestions are welcome.

Judging by the literature, most of this work has been done by Chinese researchers, at home and abroad, so this section focuses mainly on Chinese groups. First, a note: because electromagnetic waves and sound waves are alike, similar metamaterials (sometimes called photonic crystals) can be designed to modulate light. In fact, optical metamaterials appeared well before acoustic ones. Many of the groups working on acoustic metamaterials actually started out in optics and then tried, as a side project, to see whether similar phenomena exist in acoustics.

Examples include Prof. Che Ting Chan of HKUST

(http://www.phys.ust.hk/ctchan/),

Prof. Baile Zhang of Nanyang Technological University (https://www.ntu.edu.sg/home/blzhang/index.html)

and Andrea Alù of the City University of New York (CUNY)

(http://www.alulab.org/),

among others. Take Prof. Chan: [1] is a short review of topological photonic crystals that he wrote himself this year. [2] introduces some basic concepts of topological materials from an acoustics perspective, and it makes for refreshing reading. [3] discusses Dirac cones and Dirac-like cones in photonic and acoustic crystals. (A Dirac cone is a point where the valence and conduction bands touch at the Fermi level, near which the dispersion relation is approximately linear. Materials whose band structure contains Dirac cones are called Dirac semimetals; the best known is single-layer graphene.)

Another HKUST heavyweight worth mentioning is Prof. Ping Sheng

(http://sheng.people.ust.hk/?page_id=271).

In his early career he specialized in graphene and carbon nanotubes in condensed matter physics and made his name there; later his interests broadened to take in acoustics, optics and soft matter. I did my undergraduate thesis project in his group, on acoustic metamaterials. (A quick plug here for Jingyin [“Silence”] Technology, the acoustics company founded by Prof. Sheng’s students (https://acousticmetamaterials.org/), which specializes in designing high-efficiency sound-absorbing acoustic metamaterials. According to a former labmate, they are short of acoustics talent, so anyone interested can contact them directly.) Ping Sheng has collaborated a good deal with Prof. Che Ting Chan on acoustic metamaterials. Their 2000 paper in Science [10], for example, is one of the earliest papers on acoustic metamaterials. In addition, the review [4] by Ping Sheng and Prof. Guancong Ma of Hong Kong Baptist University is well worth reading. It starts from the theoretical foundations of acoustic metamaterials (elastic moduli, acoustic resonance and so on), works through their many applications, and goes all the way to the new directions that concepts borrowed from condensed matter, such as topological insulators, may open up for materials research.

It is worth noting that many of the groups in China working on topological acoustic metamaterials trace their lineage back to HKUST. Guancong Ma, mentioned above, was a student of Che Ting Chan, and he too has simulated many condensed matter concepts, such as the one-dimensional SSH model [2] and the Zak phase [5], non-Abelian transitions [6], non-Hermitian systems and more. Others who have worked on acoustic and photonic topology include Prof. Meng Xiao, Prof. Zhengyou Liu and Prof. Chunyin Qiu of Wuhan University, and Prof. Feng Li and Prof. Jiuyang Lu of South China University of Technology.

Beyond the large HKUST family, there are of course groups scattered across other universities working on acoustic topological structures: Baile Zhang and Andrea Alù, already mentioned, and Prof. Xuefeng Zhu of Huazhong University of Science and Technology. At Nanjing University there are Prof. Minghui Lu of the College of Engineering and Applied Sciences (https://lbgm.nju.edu.cn), and Prof. Xiaojun Liu and Prof. Ying Cheng of the School of Physics. Xiaojun Liu and Ying Cheng have recently collaborated a good deal with Prof. Johan Christensen of Universidad Carlos III de Madrid, publishing papers on acoustic second-order topological insulators [7], pseudospin-induced topological corner states [8] and non-Hermitian second-order acoustic topological insulators [9]. Notably, non-Hermitian systems have recently become a hot topic in condensed matter physics too, because non-Hermiticity means the system exchanges energy with its surroundings, which is a more realistic setting than a closed system.

Some unapologetically personal hot takes

Everything below is purely my own opinion, and I’m fully prepared to be put right by the experts.

First, imitating the research paradigms of condensed matter physics and borrowing its concepts can undoubtedly give acoustic metamaterials new ideas, and can help optimize the design of application-oriented acoustic devices. In [8], for example, the authors used robust edge states for acoustic imaging and tested how stable they remain when defects are present. Still, I think the field is at a fairly early stage of development. Most of the papers I found still rely on ingenious metamaterial designs to search for topological phenomena already known in mathematics or condensed matter physics. In other words, acoustic systems may indeed reveal phenomena that are hard to observe in electronic or photonic systems (just as solid-state materials realize, as quasiparticles, Majorana fermions that do not exist in reality). But for now the field cannot offer good predictions, and it cannot “give back” to either mathematics or condensed matter physics, in the same way that Majorana fermions in solids, even if they exist, have little to do with real high-energy particle physics. Frankly, even on the application side, apart from [8] above, I have seen almost no relevant literature. No wonder I heard that the condensed matter luminary Prof. Xiao-Gang Wen once scoffed at the field, dismissing it as “riding the hype.” I can understand Prof. Wen’s frustration, which rests on the fact that acoustic topology research will most likely never give back to condensed matter physics, but that is no reason to overlook its value for acoustics. Borrowing concepts across disciplines is actually very common in science. Condensed matter physics itself has borrowed plenty from elsewhere: the concept of topology from mathematics, the creation and annihilation of particles from quantum field theory, and so on. I still hope this kind of research will help bring about new acoustic devices that make people’s lives easier.

Acknowledgments

I thank Fanyu Meng and Er Mu, my seniors in the field, for providing this excellent platform for sharing knowledge about acoustics, and Dr. Liu for valuable suggestions on revising this series.

About the author: jemand has a bachelor’s degree in physics from Nanjing University, is studying for a master’s in physics at RWTH Aachen University, and will probably end up working in acoustics. That’s all.
